summary: This Wikipedia-derived note covers Thuringia's demographics, its political history, its agriculture, and its settlement and population trends. It reports that foreign residents numbered 41,000 in July 2013 (1.9%), with the largest citizenship groups being Russians, Poles, Vietnamese, Turks and Ukrainians. It traces Thuringia's formation from many small duchies and principalities into one state in 1920, and notes that agriculture is still relatively important there and that cities have grown while rural villages have declined.
one_line: Overview of Thuringia's migration figures, 19th-20th century political history, agricultural output, and urban-rural population trends.
key_facts: In July 2013, there were 41,000 non-Germans by citizenship living in Thuringia, or 1.9% of the population.
The number of non-German residents in Thuringia rose from 33,000 in July 2011, an increase of 24% in two years.
About 4% of Thuringia's population are migrants, including persons who already received German citizenship.
As of 2012, the largest foreign citizenship groups in Thuringia were Russians (3,100), Poles (3,000), Vietnamese (2,800), Turks (2,100) and Ukrainians (2,000).
The college towns Erfurt, Jena, Weimar and Ilmenau have the highest rates of foreign residents in Thuringia.
The Thuringian states were included in the Napoleonic Confederation of the Rhine, organized in 1806.
The 1815 Congress of Vienna confirmed the Thuringian states' inclusion in the German Confederation.
In 1920, after World War I, the small Thuringian states merged into one state called Thuringia; only Saxe-Coburg voted to join Bavaria instead.
Weimar became the new capital of Thuringia in 1920.
54% of Thuringia's territory is in agricultural use.
Important fruit products include apples, strawberries, cherries and plums; important vegetables include cabbage, potatoes, cauliflower, tomatoes, onions, cucumbers and asparagus.
During the Middle Ages, Thuringia was situated at the border between Germanic and Slavic territories, marked by the Saale river.
The Ostsiedlung movement led to the assimilation of Slavic people between the 11th and 13th centuries under German rule.
Since 1990, Thuringia's population has been in decline, after growing through the 18th century and staying high until World War I.
Many Thuringian villages lost half of their population since 1950, whereas the biggest cities, Erfurt and Jena, keep growing.
